clue.text: What made St Francis love his work?

definitions.text: What made St Francis love his work?

parts.words: What made St Francis love his work?
parts.note: reads like a question about job satisfaction, but points to the devotion to Christ's suffering that drove the saint, who even bore the stigmata

explanation.surface: A curious question about why a medieval friar enjoyed his vocation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' hides the word passion and 'his work' is Christ's suffering on the cross, which St Francis of Assisi was devoted to.
explanation.definitionFit: Christ's suffering and death are known as the Passion, the devotion that inspired St Francis.

clue.text: Quality 3 won by 14

parts.note: water means quality, as in a gem 'of the first water'
the answer to 3 begins with a word for a lavatory, and loo is another

explanation.surface: A note that some quality was earned by a numbered entrant.
explanation.walkthrough: '3' stands for its answer's first word, JOHN, a slang lavatory, so it gives LOO; 14 is WELLINGTON, the Duke who won the battle.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1815 battle at Waterloo was the Duke of Wellington's great victory over Napoleon.

clue.text: Good speller gets a spot of relief with spring in footwear

parts.note: a john is a lavatory, a place where one relieves oneself
a wellington is a rubber boot
wells are springs of water

explanation.surface: Someone with a talent for spelling gets their feet into some springy boots.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on spells: John Wellington Wells is the dealer in magic in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera The Sorcerer, not a good spellchecker.
explanation.definitionFit: The character is a sorcerer who sells magic potions, so he is literally a caster of spells.

clue.text: No use being without 14s

definitions.meaning: an old word meaning futile or to no avail
lacking wellingtons, that is boots, read literally

explanation.definitionFit: Bootless means unavailing, while the word broken up means having no boots, as wellingtons are.

clue.text: Attack causing fool to suffer

parts.note: an ass is a fool
to ail is to suffer illness

explanation.surface: An assault that leaves an idiot in pain.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail is a verb meaning to attack violently, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Poet's father rounds up captive of little value

indicators.note: the father's letters go round the turned captive, enclosing it

parts.note: the poet Tennyson read as Tenny's son, making Tenny his father

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read bottom to top

parts.note: a POW is a prisoner of war

explanation.surface: A poet's dad gathers up a prisoner who is worth very little.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that Tennyson read as Tenny's son makes Tenny the poet's father; 'up' turns the captive over in this down entry, and 'rounds' puts it inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Twopenny describes something cheap and trivial, worth only a couple of pence.

clue.text: Sad song for ordinary time

parts.note: plain means ordinary or unadorned

explanation.surface: A mournful tune chosen for a normal occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaint is a lament, a mournful complaint often sung or recited.

clue.text: Gracious pilgrim's reasonable return has to acquire some ardour to be very ardent

parts.note: Robert Aske led the Pilgrimage of Grace, the 1536 rising against Henry VIII

indicators.note: the word for reasonable is read backwards, coming back

parts.note: sane means reasonable
must means has to

indicators.note: only part of the word ardour is used, its opening letters

explanation.surface: A kindly pilgrim's sensible comeback needs a dash of passion to be truly fervent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns SANE into ENAS; 'some' takes ARD from ardour. 'Gracious' is not kindly but refers to the Pilgrimage of Grace.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone extremely eager and enthusiastic, mustard being sharp and pungent.

clue.text: Partially similar to us French holding a record

indicators.note: the French phrase holds the other pieces within it

parts.note: in French, 'to us' is à nous
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: Something a bit like the French version of ourselves keeps hold of a document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to us' is translated as À NOUS (accent dropped), which 'holding' wraps round A LOG.
explanation.definitionFit: Analogous things correspond in some respects but not all, so they are alike in part.

clue.text: See 3
Butter producer a crazy lady?

parts.note: she stands for a woman
a nut is a crazy person

explanation.surface: Asking whether a woman who makes butter is mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'a crazy lady' as 'she [is] a nut'. The butter is shea butter, a vegetable fat, not dairy.
explanation.definitionFit: The shea nut yields shea butter, a fat used in cooking and cosmetics.

clue.text: Tell what they say is for a winner

indicators.note: signals that the words are spoken, so their sound is what counts

parts.note: what a winner gets is a prize

explanation.surface: A statement about what people say a victor receives.
explanation.definitionFit: To apprise someone is to inform them, a formal synonym for tell.

clue.text: Make eyes at topless goblin

indicators.note: the goblin word loses its top, its first letter

parts.note: a bogle is a goblin or bogey in Scottish and northern folklore

explanation.surface: Ogling a goblin that has its top off.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to stare amorously, the same as making eyes at someone.

clue.text: See 3
Alternative persons around junction of river in Syria

parts.note: or introduces an alternative

indicators.note: the word for persons goes around the junction letter

parts.note: ones means people, as in 'loved ones'
a T-junction gives T

explanation.surface: Other people gather at the confluence of a Syrian river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orontes flows through Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, so it is a river in Syria.

clue.text: Guy's number (figure)

parts.note: ten is a number
a trope is a figure of speech

explanation.surface: A man's number, with a figure noted in brackets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a man, but a guy is a rope that steadies a tent.
explanation.definitionFit: A guy is a rope or line pegged out to hold a tent in place.

clue.text: Preceding Guardian solver's rights held in divine hands

indicators.note: the solver's rights come before the newspaper's word for itself

parts.note: the setter addresses the solver as thou, so 'solver's' is thy
R is the abbreviation for right, so rights gives RS
the Guardian newspaper speaking of itself says us

explanation.surface: Readers of the Guardian come first, and their rights are guarded by the gods.
explanation.walkthrough: A thyrsus is the staff carried by Bacchus (Dionysus), so it is held by a god.
explanation.definitionFit: The thyrsus, an ivy-topped staff, is carried by the god Bacchus and his followers.

clue.text: Arboreal lichen found by English doctor in lock …

indicators.note: the English doctor is put inside the lock of hair

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair
MO is a medical officer, a doctor

explanation.surface: A tree lichen is discovered by an English physician inside a strand of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Tree moss is a name for lichens and mosses growing on trees.

clue.text: … hence house containing 10 and 14

indicators.note: from that, meaning the letters of the previous answer are worked into a new order

parts.note: the dots carry on from 17, whose answer supplies the letters

explanation.surface: Continuing from the lichen: so it follows that a home holds two numbered places.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots link to 17 down; 'hence' rearranges its answer TREE MOSS. Wells (10) and Wellington (14) are both towns in Somerset, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset, the county in southwest England, houses both the towns of Wells and Wellington.

clue.text: Capital under 14

definitions.meaning: the name of the horse the Duke of Wellington rode at Waterloo

explanation.definitionFit: Copenhagen is Denmark's capital and was also the Duke of Wellington's famous charger.

clue.text: Spot politician in large building

indicators.note: the politician is placed inside the building

parts.note: a pile is a large imposing building
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Seeing a politician in a huge mansion.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimple is a spot on the skin, a common synonym.

clue.text: Drink at quiet river in Syria

parts.note: ale is a drink
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, quiet
the Po is Italy's longest river

explanation.surface: Having a beer by a calm river in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'river in Syria' tempts as the definition as in 15, but Aleppo is a city; the river is the Po.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleppo is a major city in northern Syria, so it is something found there.

clue.text: Unusual variety of bird helps to raise me up

indicators.note: each word lends some letters, together making up the bird's name

explanation.surface: Something that lifts my spirits is a rare bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Emeu is an old, less usual spelling of emu, the flightless Australian bird.

clue.text: Note to detective: this may follow the crime

parts.note: re is a note of the sol-fa scale
Inspector Morse is a fictional Oxford detective

explanation.surface: A memo to a detective about what comes after a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Remorse is the guilt or regret a wrongdoer may feel after committing a crime.

clue.text: Detective — this may colour what you hear

indicators.note: signals the words are judged by how they are spoken

parts.note: may plus grey, a colour

explanation.surface: A detective whose name hints at a shade when spoken.
explanation.walkthrough: Said in French, Maigret sounds like 'may grey'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Maigret is Georges Simenon's fictional Paris police detective.

clue.text: Club attached to 14's title

definitions.meaning: a golf club with a metal head

explanation.definitionFit: An iron is a type of golf club, and the Duke of Wellington was known as the Iron Duke.

clue.text: Look into juice containing 14

indicators.note: the look word goes into the juice word

parts.note: sap is the juice of a plant
lo is an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: Peering into some juice that contains a boot.
explanation.walkthrough: Salop is the old name for Shropshire, an English county containing the town of Wellington (14).
explanation.definitionFit: Shropshire, formerly Salop, includes a town called Wellington, so the county holds it.

clue.text: Committed larceny in support of person with gun

indicators.note: the theft word is placed inside the support

parts.note: a pier is a supporting pillar
stole means committed theft

explanation.surface: A thief backing up a gunman.
explanation.definitionFit: A pistoleer is someone who uses a pistol, a gunman.
